"What we've done over time is pioneer a completely new approach to autonomous driving, making it possible to bring this to a busy and complex city like London and scale it globally," he said.
'The driver took the wheel' - what was it like to ride in?
![A selfie of Zoe in the back of a driverless robotaxi, wearing a cream blouse and wearing a seatbelt.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/f47f/live/72482f90-a6b9-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
This week I became the first British journalist to travel as a customer in a self-driving Uber after hailing one via the app.
The safety driver gave me a 30-second safety briefing, and then we were off, making our way down the busy streets of central London.
For several minutes, we negotiated the traffic without incident, cruising past a busy Brexit demonstration underway outside parliament, successfully navigating traffic lights and roadworks along the way.
When a cyclist paused and waved us forward at a mini roundabout with his arm, the car complied.
But at one point the safety driver did have to take control of the car.
Just as we were pulling off, the back doors of a van parked beside us on a narrow side road appeared to swing open. The car braked sharply, an internal alarm beeped, and the driver took the wheel.
Wayve later told me it was the driver's decision to intervene and they were confident their AI system would have handled it.
The drama was all over in a couple of seconds - but it was perhaps the perfect illustration that while the industry may be in a rush, the UK's regulators are not.
Safety concerns
Earlier this year, the government and the industry had suggested that there could be fully driverless cars for hire in London by the end of 2026, but this is looking increasingly unlikely.
The Department for Transport (DfT) and the regional authority Transport for London (TfL) are responsible for overseeing the process and have faced criticism for being slow.
A DfT spokesperson said the government department was working towards a framework being put in place to ensure self-driving cars could be on the roads in 2027, but didn't give a specific date.
"These services will be introduced carefully, subject to rigorous safety testing and regulatory approval and will require local consent which can consider the potential impacts on local roads, jobs and communities," the department said in a statement.
Christina Calderator, director of transport strategy and policy at TfL, said they were "not holding up any decision" on the cars, but instead "taking time to get it right".
"This is something that's new, it's coming to London - we need to make sure it's safe," she said.
David McMullen, senior organiser for the trade union GMB, said caution needed to be taken with the roll-out of driverless cars unless people were "prepared to see unprecedented levels of social and economic disruption".
He called on TfL and the government to develop a plan that "protects drivers" and said until one was put in place, it was "premature" to move to driverless services.
![A passenger's view inside a robotaxi as it drives through London, with the hands of the safety driver not touching but around the wheel of the car, and a large black tablet with a map on it showing where the car is going.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/737/cpsprodpb/251d/live/e767d150-a6b8-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
Zoe Kleinman's view during her robotaxi ride - with a safety driver at the wheel, ready to take control if needed
Waymo - another driverless car firm owned by Google's Alphabet - has cars which have been driving London's streets for several months carrying out mapping.
These cars currently have a safety driver and members of staff in them - but are not yet for the public.
The firm says it does not intend to introduce a service that would include a human at the wheel.
Experts said there were still numerous safety challenges around self-driving cars for regulators to consider.
Prof Siddartha Khastgir, head of safe autonomy at the University of Warwick's Warwick Manufacturing Group said there were numerous safety challenges for regulators to consider.
"As human drivers we tend to make a very conscious decision of what we believe is right, and sometimes actually do things that are not perfectly legal - so for example, we tend to mount the kerb to give way to an ambulance," he said.
"So, how does a self-driving vehicle respond to emergency services? And what are the nuances of doing that in a crowded place like London?"
![A green promotional banner with black squares and rectangles forming pixels, moving in from the right. The text says: âTech Decoded: The worldâs biggest tech news in your inbox every Monday.â](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/41d3/live/348b21e0-26a8-11f0-8f57-b7237f6a66e6.png)
summary: Uber has launched the UK's first robotaxi service in London, featuring an initial fleet of 15 autonomous Ford Mustang electric vehicles equipped with Wayve AI technology. Every vehicle currently operates with a human safety driver behind the wheel ready to intervene if necessary. During a test ride by a journalist, the safety driver briefly took control after a van's doors appeared to open on a narrow side road, highlighting ongoing safety and regulatory caution.
key_points: Uber is the first company to launch self-driving minicabs in London, starting with a fleet of 15 vehicles.
Each robotaxi currently requires a human safety driver to be present and ready to take control.
Fares for the autonomous rides match standard UberX, Electric, or Comfort journeys.
Regulators like the Department for Transport and Transport for London are proceeding cautiously, aiming for a framework by 2027.
The vehicles use AI technology developed by the UK firm Wayve to analyze real-time surroundings using roof-mounted sensors.

title: Burnham tries to calm bond market fears as sell-off threatens crucial first budget
author: Jessica Elgot; Heather Stewart
content:
Andy Burnham moved to calm volatile bond markets on Wednesday as surging borrowing costs threatened to wreck plans for his government’s crucial first budget next month.
After a days-long sell-off of government bonds – and with the chancellor, John Healey, facing the prospect of sharply reduced spending power, Burnham used his first appearance at prime minister’s questions to promise decisions would be “grounded in fiscal responsibility”.
That was widely seen as an attempt to soothe investors after his statement to parliament on Tuesday, in which he made bold promises of more public control of utilities, further interventions on the cost of living and a recommitment to a 3% increase in defence spending.
While those offers were broadly welcomed by Labour MPs, Burnham was criticised by others for inflaming the sell-off. His former economic adviser, Jim O’Neill, said it was the “last thing” the markets needed.
Investors across world markets have been dumping government bonds amid fears about rising inflation, runaway deficits and competing demand for capital from tech companies on a debt-fuelled AI spending spree. The sell-off has driven up yields, or interest rates, including in the UK. At one point on Wednesday, the cost of 10-year borrowing for the government hit its highest level since 2008, at 5.29%, before easing slightly.
That is expected to be costly for Healey when the Office for Budget Responsibility draws up its budget forecasts. The independent watchdog bases its projection for bond yields on a snapshot of market interest rates taken several weeks before each budget and that is expected to be about now for Healey’s 28 October statement.
The chancellor has repeatedly stressed that fiscal discipline is the “bedrock” of government policy. He will give a speech on Monday setting out his plans for economic growth – less than six months after senior City and business figures gathered to hear his predecessor, Rachel Reeves, lay out her approach.
![A car sits among the wreckage of a missile strke](https://i.guim.co.uk/img/media/63c674a73f245031f8b4dca2c21a4f93625ba0dd/0_0_3600_2400/master/3600.jpg?width=445&dpr=1&s=none&crop=none)
In his first PMQs clash with Kemi Badenoch, Burnham blamed the Conservative leader’s party for leaving the UK vulnerable to market turmoil.
Criticising Burnham’s three-hour statement in the Commons the day before, Badenoch said: “He did not say no to a single spending request … And personally, I think it’s delightful that he wants to make everyone happy. But a prime minister needs to be a leader, not a people pleaser.”
Burnham said his budget would “stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost of living pressure on our constituents”.
Analysts believe higher interest rates on public debt could wipe out up to half of the £24bn headroom Rachel Reeves built up against Labour’s fiscal rules.
Government insiders told the Guardian they believed it would be very difficult for Healey to deliver a budget that had less than double-digit headroom, given the signal that would send to bond markets. However, that would leave him with almost no leeway for additional spending. No 10 sources declined to be drawn on what Burnham’s preferred level of headroom would be.
Healey will also have to show how the Treasury intends to fill a funding gap in defence spending and pay for Burnham’s cost of living measures, including the VAT cut on electricity bills.
Helen Miller, the director of the Institute for Fiscal Studies, said: “Debt interest is now one in every £12 the government is spending, so even relatively small changes can add up quite quickly.”
Alongside the narrowing margin for error against the rules, Miller identified two other budget headaches for Healey – the likely hit to growth forecasts from falling immigration and the demand for more spending on defence.
She said: “It’s not that any one of these things on their own are the kind of ‘hit the panic button’ moment, but when you add them all together, they do add real pressure on the government.”
Ruth Curtice, the director of the Resolution Foundation, said febrile markets meant the government would face additional scrutiny over the sustainability of the public finances.
after newsletter promotion
She added: “The risk of not facing up to the challenges has gone up, but also maybe the reward from showing that you’re serious about addressing them might have gone up too.”
The thinktank boss backed a call by Lord O’Neill for the new government to scrap the triple lock pension as a way of showing it was serious about balancing the books: “Jim O’Neill was on to something, in that part of the test for markets is, are they prepared to do politically unpopular things, in the name of trying to sort some of these fiscal problems out?”
O’Neill had been mooted as an economic adviser to Burnham but has instead gone public with criticism of the fledgling government.
A Treasury source insisted that unlike other major economies, including the US, the UK had a plan – inherited from Reeves – for reducing the deficit and bringing down debt. “To the extent that investors start looking at fiscal plans, we should start to distinguish ourselves in a positive way,” they said.
Global markets have been spooked by higher oil costs after a resumption of the Middle East conflict, resulting in higher expectations for future inflation.
Investors now believe the Bank of England will step in and raise interest rates three times, to 4.5% over the next year, to tackle inflation. That would push up mortgage costs just as Burnham hopes to cut the cost of living.
Burnham will host Emmanuel Macron for talks in No 10 on Thursday, as he begins to build his own relationships with European allies before the next stage of the UK’s reset with the EU.
The prime minister is expected to use the talks to continue pushing for greater cooperation with Europe to support British businesses and drive growth, with the French president a key figure in the government’s pursuit of a closer trading relationship.
Downing Street sources suggested that while the EU reset would not officially be on the agenda – because the responsibility for any deal lies with Brussels – it was likely to come up in the margins of the bilateral discussions.
Burnham indicated in the Commons on Tuesday that the next reset summit, which was delayed by the EU after Keir Starmer was ousted as prime minister, could be held in November.
summary: Andy Burnham attempted to reassure volatile bond markets after a days-long sell-off of government bonds threatened his government's upcoming budget. Surging borrowing costs, driven by global market fears and recent spending promises, have significantly reduced the chancellor's spending headroom. Analysts warn that rising debt interest and competing demands for capital are placing intense fiscal pressure on the Treasury ahead of the October 28 budget.
key_points: Andy Burnham promised decisions would be grounded in fiscal responsibility during his first prime minister’s questions.
The cost of 10-year government borrowing hit 5.29% before easing slightly, driven by a global bond sell-off and fears over inflation and deficits.
Higher interest rates threaten to wipe out a significant portion of the Treasury's fiscal headroom, leaving Chancellor John Healey with limited leeway.
Experts from the Institute for Fiscal Studies and Resolution Foundation highlighted compounding budget pressures, including defense spending, falling immigration, and rising debt interest.

title: Burnham pressed on economy at first PMQs as borrowing costs surge
author: Jennifer McKiernan
content:
![Andy Burnham in the House of Commons at Prime Minister's Questions. He is wearing a dark blue suit, white shirt and blue tie.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/999/cpsprodpb/1202/live/6e6ca9d0-a70b-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
- Published
Andy Burnham said his government would be "grounded in fiscal responsibility" as his first Prime Minister's Questions took place against a backdrop of rising UK borrowing costs.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch called on Burnham to say where spending would be cut and how he would deal with the UK's increasing debt, after the cost of borrowing for the UK reached a new 18-year high on Wednesday.
He blamed the previous Conservative government, saying the "turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that they left behind".
Burnham took over from Sir Keir Starmer in July before Parliament's summer recess, making Wednesday the first time he had faced the Tory leader at PMQs.
Burnham sought to stress his administration's fiscal responsibility and said ministers were taking steps to reduce debt.
He told MPs: "This will be a government grounded in fiscal responsibility. It will stick to the fiscal rules, but at the same time, we will help reduce cost-of-living pressure on our constituents, and that's the approach that we will take."
Interest rates on government bonds have been going up, with the yield on a 10-year bond at its highest level since 2008, while the yield on a 30-year bond is at its highest since 1998.
This means it costs the government more to borrow over the long term and could constrain the government's spending choices as the 28 October Budget approaches.
Burnham's PMQs debut came after he used the summer recess to tour the UK, announcing a series of eye-catching policies mainly aimed at tackling the cost of living.
On Wednesday, Badenoch said the prime minister had set out plenty of spending plans but no detail of how he would be paying the bill.
"The markets are clearly worried that we now have a spendthrift prime minister who wants to say yes to everyone but cannot tell us where the money is coming from," she said.
"He needs to pay for all his new promises and he has a choice - higher taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts.
"Yesterday he said change begins with honesty, so will he be honest and tell us: is he preparing to raise taxes again, yes or no?"
Burnham had earlier said he had already cut taxes, including VAT on energy bills and a cut in business rates for hospitality.
"I've already indicated my first moves were to cut tax, but I'm not going to do what any prime minister has done and write the budget here," he said, adding he and Chancellor John Healey had agreed on an earlier date for the Budget to reduce speculation.
In the Commons, Badenoch also raised comments from economist and cross-bench peer Lord Jim O'Neill, who had been tipped to become Burnham's chief economic adviser, but who ruled out joining Burnham's government.
Speaking to the BBC, Lord O'Neill had praised the PM for "a great first five weeks" which he said had helped lift consumer and business confidence; adding the current spike in market interest rates for government debt would force Labour to start "dealing with the triple lock" on the state pension, and "excessive" welfare spending.
Badenoch pointed to a warning from Lord O'Neill that the prime minister's tone during his Tuesday Commons debut would have unsettled investors, although the peer had also said that spike was mostly mirroring US market upheaval concerning the Iran conflict.
![Kemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons at PMQs. She is wearing a blue dress with a high collar](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1680/cpsprodpb/2e0e/live/cc402200-a6e6-11f1-b109-879e35c24276.jpg)
Kemi Badenoch speaking in the House of Commons at PMQs
"Lord O'Neill, a close friend of the prime minister, said yesterday's statement in the Commons was the last thing investors wanted to hear," Badenoch said.
"Lord O'Neill is a serious economist. He knows what he's talking about and, sure enough, yesterday the cost of government borrowing rose to its highest in 18 years.
"How does he plan to tackle the government's rising debt costs?"
Burnham replied that he and Lord O'Neill did "not always agree", before attacking Badenoch's shadow cabinet reshuffle for bringing MPs who were in the leadership team of former Conservative prime minister Liz Truss back to her front benches.
To shouts of "point-scoring!" from the Conservative side, he said: "Can I also say to her and the whole of her new shadow cabinet, the majority of whom were part of a government that lasted for 49 days, a short-lived government that crashed confidence in the economy and hammered people's mortgages.
"She took a decision at the weekend, she removed a shadow chancellor who said that the Truss mini budget was a mistake, and she replaced that shadow chancellor with one that helped to write the Truss mini budget."
In the Tory reshuffle, Andrew Griffith replaced Sir Mel Stride as shadow chancellor.
Badenoch said Burnham had not ruled out tax rises, claiming: "The reason why that budget failed was because spending was announced before the money to pay for it, which is exactly what he is doing right now."
The opposition leader went on to raise the alleged Russian attack on Leipzig airport in Germany, urging the prime minister to commit to 3% spending.
So far the new government has only committed to meeting the 3.5% spending target for defence by 2035, pushing back the interim 3% spending commitment to spring next year.
The new chancellor quit as defence secretary in June over the last government's failure to commit to a 3% increase, which proved to be the final nail in the coffin for Sir Keir's premiership.
Burnham told MPs: "The very reason I appointed this Chancellor to his position is because of his strong commitment to the defence of our country and to defence spending.
"We will fully fund the defence investment plan and at the spending review we will set out a plan to meet the Nato commitments by 2035, there is no problem with our commitment to defence."
![Thin, red banner promoting the Politics Essential newsletter with text saying, âGet the latest political analysis and big moments, delivered straight to your inbox every weekdayâ. There is also an image of the Houses of Parliament.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/6fad/live/133a6af0-dc98-11ef-bc01-8f2c83dad217.png)
Sign up for our Politics Essential newsletter to read top political analysis, gain insight from across the UK and stay up to speed with the big moments. It'll be delivered straight to your inbox every weekday.
summary: Prime Minister Andy Burnham faced Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch at his first Prime Minister's Questions amid surging UK borrowing costs that reached an 18-year high. Burnham defended his administration by emphasizing fiscal responsibility and blaming the previous Conservative government for market turbulence. Badenoch pressed Burnham on how he plans to fund his spending promises, warning that investors are unsettled by a lack of detail regarding potential tax rises, borrowing, or spending cuts.
key_points: UK borrowing costs reached a new 18-year high ahead of Prime Minister Andy Burnham's first PMQs debut.
Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch challenged Burnham to explain how he will pay for spending plans without resorting to higher taxes, more borrowing, or spending cuts.
Burnham defended his administration by pointing to his fiscal responsibility, stating they will stick to fiscal rules while helping with cost-of-living pressures.
Burnham blamed the previous Conservative government for leaving behind economic exposure that caused global market turbulence.

title: Andy Burnham risks Truss moment, warn bond market traders – live updates
author: Chris Price; Dominic Penna; Pieter Snepvangers; Tim Wallace; Tom Haynes
content:
![Andy Burnham refused to rule out increasing borrowing or taxes in the Budget next month](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/02/TELEMMGLPICT000500393264_17883543294700_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqPIbPYH9J4H2EuUPcMoVlfIx6JWGl9KG9-nKWAhu7dY4.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Andy Burnham refused to rule out increasing borrowing or taxes in the Budget next month](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/02/TELEMMGLPICT000500393264_17883543294700_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqPIbPYH9J4H2EuUPcMoVlfIx6JWGl9KG9-nKWAhu7dY4.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Andy Burnham risks a Liz Truss-style market meltdown unless he presents a credible plan to pay for his agenda, bond traders have warned.
Investors said the Prime Minister faces further spikes in borrowing costs unless he outlines tax rises or spending cuts to fund his major policies.
UK borrowing costs have surged to multi-decade highs this week amid a global bond market sell-off. However, investors are particularly concerned about Mr Burnham’s fiscal agenda before his first Budget next month.
Al Cattermole, a portfolio manager at Swiss private bank Mirabaud, said investors were “unclear” about the Prime Minister’s plans and how he would pay for them.
He said: “If you have a lack of credibility about your spending plan and how that will be funded, then you would get spikes in yields similar to [what] we saw during the Liz Truss episode.
“That was about unfunded fiscal spending. And if you get that again, then there is concern about that.”
Mr Burnham refused to rule out increasing borrowing during his first Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday despite recent market turmoil.
Jim Athey, a portfolio manager at Marlborough Investment, said: “Spending cuts are the thing the market wants to hear.
“It would go a long way if this Government were to recognise that it is a challenge that needs addressing – that the path we are on in terms of welfare spending is completely unsustainable.”
He added: “The market knows that, and the market wants to hear that the Government understands that.”
Lord Jim O’Neill said earlier that the Prime Minister must “get real” and cut public spending in order to ease pressure in the bond market.
The cost of long-term government borrowing hit its highest level since 1998 on Wednesday, increasing the strain on the public finances as John Healey, the new Chancellor, prepares for the Budget.
The 10-year gilt yield – a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money – has risen to its highest point since 2007.
Signing off...
Thank you for following along with our coverage of the bond markets
UK borrowing costs have surged to multi-decade highs this week amid a global bond market sell-off. However, investors are particularly concerned about Mr Burnham’s fiscal agenda before his first Budget next month.
The sell-off in government bonds has eased slightly, although UK borrowing costs remain close to their highest levels in almost two decades.
Yields on 10-year UK government bonds are up 0.02 percentage points at 5.24pc, having earlier climbed as high as 5.29pc.
The 30-year yield has also eased back from its morning peak, although it remains elevated.
Read more of our economic coverage here.
Homeowners brace for higher mortgage rates as borrowing costs surge
Homeowners are bracing for steeper mortgage rates after the cost of funding for lenders hit a three-year high under Labour.
Britain’s five-year swap rates – the interest rates that banks charge each other for borrowing – climbed to 4.57pc on Wednesday, their highest level since October 2023.
Two-year swap rates have climbed from 4.27pc at the end of last week to 4.47pc, their highest level since March, after the US and Israel escalated their conflict with Iran.
The surges threaten to heap fresh pressure on millions of homeowners, since the rates are used to help lenders price their mortgage offers. The average two-year fixed deal stands at 5.59pc, while a five-year deal is typically 5.63pc.
Bond market sell-off cools as oil price falls
The sell-off in government bonds has eased slightly, although UK borrowing costs remain close to their highest levels in almost two decades.
Yields on 10-year UK government bonds are up 0.02 percentage points at 5.24pc, having earlier climbed as high as 5.29pc.
The 30-year yield has also eased back from its morning peak, although it remains elevated.
The retreat has come as oil prices have fallen back from their highs, with Brent crude now down around 1pc at about $94 a barrel.
Higher energy prices have fuelled fears that inflation could remain stubborn, potentially delaying interest rate cuts by central banks.
Lale Akoner, global market strategist at eToro, warned that the bond sell-off could have further to run.
She said: “High oil and gas prices are keeping inflation worries alive, while governments and technology companies borrow heavily for AI.
“Bond yields could remain high even if economies slow, because central banks may delay rate cuts and more bonds compete for investors’ money.”
Number of children growing up in workless homes hits 1.5m
The number of children living in homes where no one is working has climbed to a 12-year high.
There were 1.54 million children living in workless households in the three months to June, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics. The data showed an increase of 68,000 compared with the same period a year earlier.
The total number of children in workless households is now at its highest level since December 2014, based on quarterly figures.
It comes amid an increase in the number of people who have started claiming benefits with no requirement to look for work since the pandemic.
Labour MP calls for ‘honest’ debate about triple lock
A former Labour minister has called for an “honest” and “grown-up” conversation about the pension triple lock.
Zubir Ahmed said the measure – which guarantees pensions rise each year in line with inflation, wage growth or 2.5pc – is a “manifesto commitment” that will be stuck to “through the course of this parliament”.
He suggested the “blunt instrument” should be debated “into the next election”. Andy Burnham has repeatedly denied he plans to call an early election where he can rewrite the Labour manifesto.
Mr Ahmed told Politics Live on BBC Two: “Millennials and Generation Z... are less wealthy and less able to get on things like the housing ladder, and live a comfortable life and have children, than the generations before them.
“Part of that conversation, perhaps into the next election and into future financial planning, is the fact that maybe the triple lock is quite a blunt instrument.
“It was appropriate for its time. Pensioner poverty has come down and there may be other ways that we can make sure pensioners who need that help, who need the security of their income rising with inflation, can be done in a more sophisticated manner.”
Pound falls in bond market turmoil
The value of the pound declined as confidence in Britain’s public finances was rocked by the recent surge in government borrowing costs.
Sterling fell by 0.1pc against the dollar to $1.35 as the yield on 10-year UK gilts hit their highest level since 2007, adding to the challenge facing finance minister John Healey ahead of his first Budget.
The pound was also 0.1pc lower versus the euro at €1.161.
The British currency also faces pressure from market expectations that both the US Federal Reserve and European Central Bank will raise interest rates this month as the Iran war threatens persistent inflation.
However, traders are only placing a 15pc chance on the Bank of England raising interest rates at its next meeting.
Burnham ‘already has Truss market meltdown’
The Prime Minister has been accused of “empty soundbites” on government borrowing as the interest rates on the public debt rise higher than they ever were under Liz Truss.
Here are some of the views from the comments section after Andy Burnham’s first Prime Minister’s Questions and you can join the debate here.
US stocks rise tentatively amid bond sell-off
Wall Street appeared to lack conviction at the start of trading following a pull-back in oil prices.
The Dow Jones Industrial Average opened 0.5pc higher at 53,016.35 as Brent crude slipped back below $95 a barrel.
The S&P 500 was up 0.1pc to 7,639.88 but the Nasdaq Composite was flat at 26,100.20 as higher energy prices kept borrowing costs at multi-decade highs.
Stop talking about ‘flexibility’ in fiscal rules, Burnham urged
Andy Burnham should stop talking about “flexibility” in the fiscal rules if he wants government borrowing costs to fall, an economist has said.
Daniel Mahoney of Nordic bank Handelsbanken said the Prime Minister needed to instead show he has “full control of spending”.
Lord Jim O’Neill, a key ally of Mr Burnham, said earlier that the Prime Minister needed to “get real” about spending and urged him to consider scrapping the triple lock.
Mr Mahoney said: “The best way to reassure the bond markets is to avoid talking about ‘flexibility’ within the fiscal rules – the markets reacted very badly to this when Mr Burnham moved into No 10.
“The markets will also be concerned by any suggestion that business is being used as a cash cow – resisting imposing further business taxes, and choosing to meet the fiscal rules in other ways, would also help.
“As Lord O’Neill has stated, the Government will need to demonstrate it has full control of spending.
“As one of Mr Burnham’s economic advisors, he highlighted the growth of both working-age and pensioner welfare spending as major challenges.
“But all savings will ultimately be political as well as economic decisions, and governments have struggled to reform both pensions and welfare in the past.”
Bond market wants Burnham to cut spending, say traders
Andy Burnham risks a Liz Truss-style bond market meltdown unless he present a credible plan to pay for his ambitious agenda, bond traders have warned.
The Prime Minister risks further spikes in interest rates on government debt if he fails to set out how he will pay for major policies, investors said.
UK borrowing costs have surged this week in a sharp bond market sell-off after the US launched fresh strikes against Iran, stoking inflation fears.
However, Mr Burnham refused to rule out tax rises or increasing borrowing during his first Prime Minister’s Questions on Wednesday.
Al Cattermole, a portfolio manager at Swiss private bank Mirabaud, which manages around £29bn of client money, said: “We are unclear as an industry what they intend to do.
“What is likely, if you have a lack of credibility about your spending plan and how that will be funded, then you would get spikes in yields similar to what we saw during the Liz Truss episode.
“That was about unfunded fiscal spending. And if you get that again, then there is concern about that.
“Obviously you should learn from history and we shouldn’t get that, but that then’s going to give speculation about inevitable tax hikes.
“So it’s that balance of credibility, growth, and where you can cut cost.”
He added: “I think if they don’t put taxes up, the market will question credibility.”
Jim Athey, a portfolio manager at Marlborough, said: “Spending cuts are the thing the market wants to hear. There would be a sentiment boost just from doing it.
“It would go a long way if this Government were to recognise that it is a challenge that needs addressing – that the path we are on in terms of welfare spending is completely unsustainable.
“The market knows that and the market wants to hear that the Government understands that.”
PM and Chancellor ‘in lockstep’ on meeting fiscal rules, says No 10
Andy Burnham and John Healey are “in lockstep” on meeting the Government’s fiscal rules, Downing Street has said.
The Prime Minister’s official spokesman said: “It’s important to point out that borrowing fell last year to its lowest level in six years and borrowing fell in the UK in 2026 more than in any other G20 country apart from Saudi Arabia and Russia.
“And as the Prime Minister also pointed out, the UK economy grew at the fastest rate in the G7 in the first half of 2026.
“Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of economic stability and national security.
“The Chancellor and the Prime Minister are in lockstep that the Government will meet the fiscal rules with a buffer against uncertainty and get borrowing down, and we are cutting the deficit faster than any other G7 economy between 2025 and 2030.”
Just Stop Oil protesters block streets outside Parliament
Around 80 Just Stop Oil protestors gathered outside Parliament to protest against the Jackdaw and Rosebank gas fields as Andy Burnham delivered his first Prime Minister’s Questions, writes Sapphire Hope.
Multiple buses and cars were jammed outside Parliament as tourists looked bewildered at the orange scene.
The Prime Minister is minded to approve the substantial Jackdaw gas field in the North Sea after coming under pressure to boost UK energy supplies, sources have told The Telegraph.
Dr Jen Murphy, from Scientists on Survival, told The Telegraph the climate situation has become more serious following the UK’s string of heatwaves.
When asked if she felt bad about the disruption caused by the protest, she said: “Under normal circumstances, disruption is to be avoided, but these aren’t normal circumstances, this is an absolute emergency and it is catastrophic.
“Every year is going to be hotter and hotter.
“People are calling it a new normal, it’s not normal, it is new but this going to go on.”
![Just Stop Oil protesters outside Parliament](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/02/TELEMMGLPICT000500406314_17883516177210_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqwMpl-Jpdv5EMZZkofEupHEikPYR0xYwuEBLwP9UFqPg.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
![Activists were arrested as roads were closed  in Westminster](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/09/02/TELEMMGLPICT000500406509_17883516633620_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqqVzuuqpFlyLIwiB6NTmJwVSYfRx-a0rm-wOQ3-QTCoU.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Burnham ‘between a rock and a hard place’ on borrowing costs
Andy Burnham needs to bring down public spending on the NHS or pensions to balance the nation’s books, an analyst has said.
Mike Bell, head of market strategy at RBC BlueBay Asset Management, said the Prime Minister will have “no easy solution” to bring down borrowing costs in the first Budget under his government.
He said the latest spike in energy prices and borrowing costs had come at a “hugely unhelpful” time, with the Government under huge pressure to deliver increases in the minimum wage and public sector pay as households grapple with soaring inflation.
“They need to bring borrowing costs down,” he said. “And the problem is you’ve just got such significant upward pressure on the primary deficit over the coming years because the population is going to age.
“You basically need to tackle healthcare spending but we all know there’s absolutely no way they’re going to do that.
“There’s no way they’re going to say we need to cut spending on the NHS or means test the NHS.
“A smaller thing that they could do is get rid of the triple lock. It’s not the main thing that needs doing, but it would be helpful.
“But again, it’s political suicide to get rid of the triple lock going into a another spike in food and energy prices when you’ve got so many pensioners who go out and vote.
“So they’re just between a rock and a hard place basically.”
Senior Labour MP attacks Burnham’s defence delay
One of Labour’s most senior backbench MPs has attacked Andy Burnham’s refusal to commit to spending 3 per cent of GDP on defence by 2030.
Mr Burnham and John Healey, the Chancellor, will not set out a pathway to reaching 3 per cent of the nation’s gross domestic product on the military until the spending review next year, and have refused to confirm that it will be reached by 2030.
Tan Dhesi, the Labour chairman of the defence select committee, said: “The British people should be under no illusion that the nation faces a significantly increased threat level especially from Russia but also we have a US leadership for whom European security is no longer a focus or priority.
“And that is why it is imperative that we invest in our Armed Forces in the here and now rather than be sorry later. Indeed, defence is definitely one area where vibes alone just isn’t going to be enough.
“So rather than kick the can down the road, waiting for a fiscal event in a future year, will the Prime Minister urgently commit to charting a pathway to reach 3 per cent of GDP spend on defence by 2030, which as his Chancellor rightly noted is critical to keep our country safe?”
Mr Burnham responded: “Well I’ve made that commitment, made it very clear, and I have done for a considerable period of time. And I was in Ukraine last week for a specific reason, to repeat it on the world stage there so the Honourable gentleman can be absolutely sure of that. But I think as well as our commitment to our defence we also have to build the resilience of Britain.”
Burnham: I support ‘broken windows’ approach to policing
Andy Burnham has declared that he backs the US-inspired “broken windows” philosophy on tackling crime.
Kim Leadbeater, the Labour backbench MP, asked Mr Burnham what steps he would take to support people in communities like Spen Valley, in her constituency, where people were “dealing with antisocial behaviour” such as speeding and dangerous driving.
Mr Burnham replied: “She’s speaking for many people at home who will be nodding away when she says what she’s said. I spoke to these issues in the Makerfield by-election where we had an illegal waste tip that just looked like no-one was taking any action on.
“Fireworks, I think there is a case for going further, regulating those. But on antisocial behaviour more broadly, I supported Greater Manchester Police in taking the toughest possible approach to antisocial behaviour through Operation Vulcan. I think it can be extended elsewhere.
“We shouldn’t accept that this is just the daily norm in communities. I happen to support the ‘broken window’ theory of policing, if you let small things go, bigger things come along, and we should change the way we think about neighbourhood policing, as the Home Secretary is doing.”
Burnham: ‘Imperative’ Britain becomes closer to the EU
Andy Burnham said it was “imperative” that Britain becomes closer to the European Union in the coming years.
Sir Ed Davey, the Liberal Democrat leader, urged the Prime Minister to rejoin the EU single market, claiming it was “the bold step our country desperately needs”.
Mr Burnham responded: “The decade of low growth has been partly a result of Brexit and sooner the party opposite accepts that, the more we can start to face up to Britain’s future and where do we go from here.
“I do want a closer relationship, I will build on the work on my predecessor. There are issues facing British farming right now and there are issues facing British Steel right now. And the ‘made in Europe’ agenda could pose significant problems for British Steel.
“So as he will know we are approaching a UK-EU summit in the next couple of months. It is imperative, I believe, that we work hard to get a good deal for British Steel, for British farming, as part of that new deal that he talks about.”
Andy Burnham: My plan is based on ‘positivity and possibility’
Andy Burnham said his plan for the economy was based on “positivity” and “possibility”.
The Prime Minister claimed Britain was “heading in the right direction” on his watch, telling his first PMQs: “Yesterday, I laid out a clear, coherent plan for growth based on 10 years of delivering it myself.
“This is grounded in reality, I want to take it to all parts of the country and it’s all about bringing back a sense of positivity, a sense of possibility, growth in every postcode.
“Let this country believe in itself again, let people have some hope. And that is what this Government will do.”
Burnham refuses to commit to 3 per cent on defence by 2030
Andy Burnham has refused to commit to including a 3 per cent defence target for 2030 in next year’s spending review.
John Healey, who is now the Chancellor, resigned as defence secretary in June over Sir Keir Starmer’s failure to pledge to spend 3 per cent of GDP on the military by 2030. However, Mr Burnham’s Government is now refusing to make the same commitment.
Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, said: “I asked him if he would rule out more borrowing, he did not do so. We spend more servicing our debt than we do on our defence, almost double. There is war in Europe. Yesterday, Germany confirmed that Russia was behind the attack on Leipzig airport. Tensions are so high the director of the CIA flew to Moscow.
“We need the plan to hit 3 per cent on defence now, but the Armed Forces won’t know what they’ll be getting until next July’s spending review. There is a simple answer to this, cut welfare spending and invest that money in our defence now. The honeymoon is over. Isn’t it time for the Prime Minister to ditch the vibes and get serious about defence spending?”
Mr Burnham responded by saying that the German government’s announcement “should unite the House in sending complete condemnation of that attack by Russia and completely solidarity” with Russia and Ukraine.
He continued: “The very reason I appointed this Chancellor to his position is because of his strong commitment to the defence of our country and defence spending. We will fully fund our Defence Investment Plan and at the spending review we will set out a plan to meet our Nato commitments by 2035. There is no problem with our commitment to defence.”
Burnham refuses to rule out more borrowing
Andy Burnham has refused to rule out more government borrowing despite the market chaos of the past few days.
Kemi Badenoch said the cost of borrowing was “far more than it ever was under Liz Truss”, telling MPs: “The reason why that Budget failed is because spending was announced before the money to pay for it which is exactly what he is doing right now. He says it’s the new politics, it’s the same old Labour politics, tax and spend.
“He did not rule out tax rises and what markets see is a government that cannot control its spending, so the markets will charge us more for borrowing... Higher borrowing costs are the biggest threat to family finances, so can he rule out any more borrowing that will make people poorer?”
Mr Burnham replied: “Debt was rising as a percentage of GDP under the government that she served in and her new shadow chancellor served in, who was hardly some PPS to the Defra Secretary with all respect to my honourable friend, the Defra Secretary. He was in the Treasury as a senior minister on the day of the Truss budget.
“She mentions mortgage rates, well that was the day that they spiked and that was the day the British public was hammered by the previous government. We are taking the action needed to get debt down, this will be a Government grounded in fiscal responsibility, it will stick to the fiscal rules but at the same time we will help reduce cost of living pressure on our constituents and that’s the approach that we will take.”
Burnham refuses to rule out Budget tax rises
Andy Burnham refused to rule out further tax rises at John Healey’s first Budget next month.
Kemi Badenoch, the Conservative leader, said: “The markets are clearly worried that we now have a spendthrift Prime Minister who wants to say yes to everyone but cannot tell us where the money is coming from.
“He needs to pay for all his new promises and he has a choice: higher taxes, more borrowing or spending cuts. Yesterday, he said change begins with honesty. So will he be honest and tell us is he preparing to raise taxes again, yes or no?”
Mr Burnham said: “I’ve already indicated my first moves were to cut tax but I’m not going to do what any Prime Minister has done and is write the Budget here. That would be the matter for my Right Honourable friend...
“But can I also say to her and indeed to the whole of her new shadow cabinet, the majority of whom were part of a government that lasted for 49 days, a short-lived government that crashed confidence in the economy, hammered people’s mortgages. She took a decision at the weekend, she removed a shadow chancellor who said that the Truss mini-budget was a mistake and she replaced that shadow chancellor with one that helped write the Truss mini-budget and dare I remind the House that the leader of the Opposition is on record as saying that Liz Truss is 100 per cent right? What other thing can I say... other than God help us?”
Burnham refuses to say how he will tackle soaring debt
Andy Burnham has refused to say how he intends to tackle the Government’s soaring debt costs.
Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, told the Prime Minister: “Lord O’Neill, a close friend of the Prime Minister, said yesterday’s statement in the Commons was the last thing investors wanted to hear.
“Lord O’Neill is a serious economist, he knows what he’s talking about and sure enough, yesterday, the cost of government borrowing rose to its highest in 18 years. How does he plan to tackle the Government’s rising debt costs?”
Mr Burnham replied: “Can I say to the Right Honourable lady, I’ve worked with Jim O’Neill for 10 years. Jim O’Neill always gives me candid advice, we don’t always agree. But he and I worked together to turn Greater Manchester from a former industrial heartland to the fastest-growing city region in the country.
“They complain, but where are their ideas about growth? When they were in government we saw 14 years of stagnant growth, we saw 14 years of debt rising as a percentage of GDP. I would say to her that the turbulence on global markets are because of that exposure that we left behind. We are turning that corner.”
Mr Burnham said Britain had the fastest growth in the G7 and that borrowing fell to its lowest level in six years in the first half of 2026, adding: “I say to the party opposite... that is problem-solving rather than pointscoring.”
Badenoch: Burnham wants to cut welfare by spending more money
Kemi Badenoch has accused Andy Burnham of wanting to bring welfare costs down by spending more money.
The Tory leader said: “Personally I think it’s delightful that he wants to make everyone happy but a Prime Minister needs to be a leader, not a people-pleaser. He’s talking about working together on welfare. I already made that offer but that does mean cuts. He wants to bring the welfare bill down by spending more money.
“Yesterday, the Prime Minister told the House that his promises would be paid for by reprioritising within government. So what exactly has he cut?”
Mr Burnham replied: “Well, in terms of ‘what has he cut?’, tax is the simple answer to that question. Within days of taking office I indicated that we would remove VAT off electricity bills, and that will help people with the cost of living. And then days later with the support of my Right Honourable friend the Chancellor, we said that there would be a cut in business rates for pubs, social clubs, live music venues.
“So this Government lowering the cost of living, lowering the cost of business, and that is what we will continue to do. And can I say to the Right Honourable lady, it has to be fully-funded and those commitments are fully-funded and we made a decision, early, to be clear about our priorities. Digital ID is not a priority for me or for this government, we reallocated the funding and we made those commitments as a result.”
Mr Burnham’s remarks came despite Darren Jones, who oversaw Sir Keir Starmer’s flagship digital ID policy, stating that the funding for the policy had never been found by Sir Keir’s Government.
I can’t defend Neet numbers, admits Prime Minister
Andy Burnham said he “can’t defend” the number of young people not in education, employment or training.
Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader, told the Prime Minister: “Yesterday, he faced 125 questions from MPs across the House. Of course, Labour and the Lib Dems just wanted more government spending as taxpayers’ money. But can he name a single spending request to which he answered no?”
Mr Burnham replied: “What I can say to the Right Honourable lady is I was quite clear in my statement about the need to get the welfare bill down. I do not want to be a Prime Minister that sees a situation where we have so many people in their 20s not in education, employment or training. I can’t defend that.
“And I want to change that by giving more support to young people, so we start investing in their success rather than paying for failure as we have done for many years under successive governments. Now this seems to me to be one area where we can both engage in problem-solving rather than point-scoring and I hope the Right Honourable lady will take up my offer on that point.”
Burnham declines to apologise over early release
Andy Burnham declined to apologise for “months of anguish for bereaved families” following his about-turn on the early release scheme.
Mr Burnham was asked by Ann Davies, the MP for Caerfyrddin: “Will the Prime Minister now apologise to victims and their families put through significant distress throughout this process, and can he also assure them that unlike the Labour precedent there will be no Government U-turn on this?”
Mr Burnham responded: “Can I say I do understand their anguish and that of many other families who found themselves in their position. I listened to what they were saying, I came in and asked for changes to the early release scheme and we excluded rape, grooming and child sex offences.
“But hearing those voices I wasn’t satisfied and I pushed the system to go further and as a result of that we are going further and excluding death by dangerous and other manslaughter offences. So I hope now she can give that certainty to the family, give them also my best wishes. I believe we’re coming to the right position and I can assure her that the Justice Secretary will be on top of this situation so we can ensure we are never in this position again.”
Burnham looks forward to Bayeux Tapestry
Andy Burnham used the start of his first PMQs to look ahead to the arrival of the Bayeux Tapestry at the British Museum.
The Prime Minister said: “It was good to be back at this dispatch box yesterday for the first time in 16 years and I understand I broke records on my first day back for the longest statement in modern history. Thanks for your help with that, Mr Speaker.
“On my engagements, this evening I will join Their Majesties the King and Queen and president Macron at the British Museum to celebrate the arrival of the Bayeux Tapestry. The loaning of the Tapestry is a great example of French-British cooperation, the same cooperation that has helped us reduce small boat crossings to a seven-year low.
“This morning I had meetings with ministerial colleagues and others. In addition to my duties in this House, I will have further such meetings later today.”
Jenrick: Burnham must use PMQs to pledge spending cuts
Andy Burnham must use his first PMQs to pledge that he and John Healey will cut spending, Robert Jenrick has said.
Mr Jenrick, Reform UK’s Treasury spokesman, said: “The Government urgently needs to get borrowing and inflation under control. That means supply side reform, but it also requires an immediate fiscal response.
“Andy Burnham must use PMQs to send a clear signal to the markets that he will cut wasteful spending. Reform has announced a plan to cut £50 billion out of the working-age welfare budget.
“It’s a no brainer for Healey to adopt our plan at his upcoming budget to give the country breathing space. If he doesn’t act, the country is going to be paying the price with more and more of people’s taxes spent just servicing our debt.”
I want to ‘rethink’ PMQs, says Burnham
Andy Burnham will also answer questions from his social media followers once he has taken his first PMQs.
In a video posted to his Instagram story, the Prime Minister claimed that he wanted to “do it differently” ahead of his showdown with Kemi Badenoch, the Tory leader.
Mr Burnham said: “We’re going to rethink PMQs and do it differently and I want to be talking to you, to the public, rather than just to the House of Commons.
“So let’s make it ‘People’s Major Questions’, rather than Prime Minister’s Questions, and send me what you want to ask me and I’ll answer them after the other PMQs tomorrow.”
Burnham faces PMQs showdown over bond market rout
Andy Burnham will have to answer for Britain’s soaring borrowing costs when he faces Kemi Badenoch at his first PMQs.
The Prime Minister is to take questions in the Commons at midday after a marathon question-and-answer session on Tuesday was overshadowed by a surge in gilt yields.
Britain’s borrowing costs have risen at one of the fastest paces in the world and interest rates on 10-year gilts, a benchmark for the Treasury, are at their highest level since 2008.
The market stress will leave Mr Burnham up to £14bn short at his first Budget next month, hampering his plans for an increase in state spending.
Labour on ‘collision course’ with bond markets
Labour is on a “collision course” with the bond markets, a shadow minister has warned.
Louie French, a Tory frontbencher shadowing the department for culture, media and sport, warned that Andy Burnham was doing nothing to silence the “alarm bells” over soaring borrowing costs.
Mr French said: “Alarm bells are ringing in the City and Treasury as investors react to the perilous state of the UK’s finances.
“Andy Burnham’s response is a ‘triple helix approach’ to the economy. Labour are on a collision course with the bond markets they thought could be ignored.”
In his first Commons statement on Tuesday, Mr Burnham said his “triple helix” on the economy would combine “business, academia and government”.
Long-term borrowing costs highest since 1998
Britain’s long-term cost of borrowing has surpassed 5.9pc for the first time in 28 years as the bond market rout deepens.
The yield on 30-year gilts hit a 28-year high of 5.91pc on Wednesday, rising by 0.06 percentage points, as fears grow about a persistent inflation as a result of the Iran war.
Meanwhile, the 10-year gilt yield has climbed as much as 0.07 percentage points to 5.29pc, its highest level since 2007.
Daniel Mahoney, senior UK economist at Handelsbanken, said: “The 10-year gilt yield has hit levels last seen during the global financial crisis.
“Recent drivers of increasing gilt yields have been broadly international – including geopolitical risk and competition for investor capital in the context of the AI boom – but it continues to be a major concern that UK government borrowing costs remain notably higher than G7 counterparts.”
He added: “Current moves in financial markets are clearly set to further erode the Government’s fiscal headroom at the upcoming Budget, adding to the likelihood that fresh tax increases will be announced on October 28.”
Burnham urged to cut benefits before the triple lock
Telegraph readers told the Prime Minister to cut spending on this “less worthy” as surging borrowing costs put pressure on the public finances.
Here are some of the views from the comments section below and you can join the debate here.
Burnham urged to avoid wealth taxes
Andy Burnham has been urged not to impose a wealth tax or raise the rate of capital gains tax by his former economic advisor.
Lord O’Neill, who turned down a role in Mr Burnham’s government, urged the Prime Minister to reform capital gains tax by offering “incentives” for entrepreneurs and “real” risk takers.
He added some assets were being “gamed” and should be taxed at the same rate as income.
He told Times Radio: “I would personally be very opposed to any increase in capital gains tax but I can see the case for a proper reform.”
While he signalled his support for a land value tax, he said any other form of wealth tax “would not be a smart thing to do”, adding: “It would just result in even more people probably deciding to leave the country, and act as a disincentive to business.”
Interest rates expected to rise three times as Iran war drags on
UK borrowing costs are rising as investors expect the war in the Middle East to force the Bank of England to raise interest rates.
Money markets indicate policymakers will raise rates three times over the next year, from 3.75pc to 4.5pc, with two hikes priced in by February.
It comes as the renewed strikes in Iran raise doubts about the conflict coming to an end, threatening to fuel inflation.
It has helped drive the 10 and 30-year gilt yields to their highest levels since 2007 and 1997, respectively.
Matthew Amis, investment director at Aberdeen Investments, said: “Gilt yields look elevated here but until oil and gas start freely moving in the Straits of Hormuz, gilt yields are going to struggle.
“On the politics front, PM Burnham delivered his maiden speech to parliament yesterday.
“From a gilt market perspective, I don’t think we learnt anything new. But what is clear is with gilt yields at these levels, the fiscal room for manoeuvre going into October’s budget is incredibly limited.”
Mortgage rates poised to soar as borrowing costs rise
Mortgage rates are poised to rise sharply after costs for lenders hit a three-year high.
Five-year swap rates – the interest rates that banks charge each other for borrowing – climbed to 4.57pc on Wednesday, which is their highest level since October 2023.
Two-year swap rates have climbed from 4.27pc at the end of last week to 4.47pc, their highest level since March, following the escalation of the conflict in the Middle East.
The rates are used to help lenders price their mortgage products. The average two-year fixed deal stands at 5.59pc, while a five-year deal is typically 5.63pc.
Rachel Springall of Moneyfacts said: “This does not bode well for borrowers, as lenders use swap rates as a key influence to reprice their fixed-rate mortgages.
“Those borrowers who were hoping for cheaper mortgage rates will be frustrated if lenders start hiking rates over the coming weeks, so it is essential borrowers seek advice and secure a new deal quickly.
“The renewed pressure on swap rates comes as the escalating military conflict between the US and Iran reignites inflation fears, with Brent crude oil prices rising amid threats to supply routes through the Strait of Hormuz.
“A global bond sell-off has also pushed the UK 10-year gilt yield above 5.2pc, its highest level since 2008, increasing pressure on the wholesale funding costs that underpin fixed mortgage pricing.”
Burnham urged to ‘get real’ on triple lock to win over markets
Andy Burnham must “get real” and cut public spending to win back market confidence, his former economic adviser has said.
Lord O’Neill, a former minister and Goldman Sachs economist who turned down an offer to join Mr Burnham’s Government, urged the Prime Minister to consider scrapping the state pension triple lock or lowering “excessive” welfare spending.
It comes after the bond markets reacted negatively to Mr Burnham’s debut in the Commons on Tuesday in a rout that sent borrowing costs to their highest level since 2008.
Speaking to BBC Radio 4, Lord O’Neill warned that current market pressure meant Mr Burnham would be forced to take control of public spending.
He said: “It’s going to force his own political party and hopefully the whole Whitehall system to get real about dealing with some of the things that are out there, such as the triple lock, excessive spending on welfare.”
He later told Times Radio: “What this boils down to, he’s got to make some cuts in terms of government spending.”
“There’s been a denial from all sorts of governments, the many of which we’ve had the past few years, where they just sort of live in a world where none of these things seem to be real, and it’s got into this psychology where they’re sort of regarded as sacred cows that no politician dare touch.”
The market reaction poses another headache for Mr Burnham as he prepares to face Kemi Badenoch in his first appearance at Prime Minister’s Questions at 12pm.
Addressing MPs for the first time since entering No 10, Mr Burnham claimed that “life is too expensive and too hard for too many”, blaming Brexit and Margaret Thatcher for “low growth and stalled regeneration”.
UK bonds ‘especially exposed’ to Iran conflict
Britain’s borrowing costs are more susceptible to sharp rises during flare ups in the Iran war, analysts have warned.
Roger Lee, head of equity strategy at Cavendish, a UK investment bank, said the state of Britain’s public finances meant it was quickly swept up in global sell-offs in the markewt.
He said: “Whilst this is very much a global sell-off in government bonds focused on countries with high deficits and/or high absolute debt levels, given the UK’s fiscal position, gilts are seen as especially exposed.
“Pressure in the bond market will amplify the UK’s fiscal challenges.
“The current level of bond yields is likely to erode most of the previous headroom leaving new PM Andy Burnham with even more complicated budget choices in October.”
European stocks fall over inflation fears
European shares hovered near a one-month low under pressure from the spike in bond yields.
The Europe-wide Stoxx 600 edged down 0.1pc as escalating tensions in the Middle East stoked worries about inflation.
Germany’s Dax and France’s Cac 40 fell 0.2pc as fresh attacks between the US and Iran sent Brent crude oil prices to a six-week high above $95 a barrel.
The yield on German 10-year bonds hit its highest since April 2011, while investors see a near 40pc chance that the European Central Bank’s deposit rate could hit 3pc by March 2027, up from a 25pc chance last week.
UK borrowing costs hit new 28-year high
The cost of long-term government borrowing has climbed to its highest level since 1998, ramping up pressure on Britain’s public finances.
The yield on 30-year UK gilts hit 5.89pc on Wednesday over concerns that the Iran war will continue to push up inflation.
The yield on 10-year gilts, a benchmark for what the Treasury pays to borrow money, rose to 5.25pc. It last reached that level in 2007.
German borrowing costs hit 15-year high
The cost of government borrowing in Europe’s largest economy has hit its highest level in 15 years as the rout in bond markets deepens.
Germany’s 10-year bund yield, a benchmark for the eurozone, rose to 3.38pc, its highest level since 2011 as trading got underway on Wednesday.
The 10-year yield in France rose to 4.25pc, its highest level since 2008, with investors now turning to what happens when UK markets open shortly.
UK bonds were the worst performers among major global economies on Tuesday, overshadowing Andy Burnham’s first appearance in the Commons as Prime Minister.
Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “The 10-year gilt yield was up 8.1 basis points on the day to 5.22pc.
“Meanwhile, the 30yr gilt yield hit a post-1998 high of 5.86pc with lots of talk about the government’s buffer against its own fiscal rules being slashed with the recent rise in yields.
“All ahead of the new leadership’s first budget on October 28th.”
Burnham will stick to ‘rigidly’ to fiscal rules
Andy Burnham will stick “rigidly” to the Government’s fiscal rules, a minister has said as borrowing costs rise.
Cabinet Office minister Sally Jameson said she disagreed with comments by Lord Jim O’Neill, an ally of the Prime Minister.
He had suggested international investors would not have approved of Mr Burnham’s “tone” in the Commons on Tuesday about “implying a lot more government spending”.
Ms Jameson told Sky News: “I think it’s important we don’t over-read into individual comments people make, because I think Andy Burnham has been really clear that we are going to stick to those fiscal rules rigidly, and that fiscal responsibility is absolutely imperative.”
She added: “We’ve got to have controls on spending, and I don’t think Andy or anyone else has said any different to that.
“But I think the key thing is having growth and bringing optimism back into this country.”
Gas prices hit three-year high over Hormuz fears
The price of wholesale gas in Europe hit a three-year high after the fresh fighting between the US and Iran, threatening further turmoil in bond markets.
Dutch TTF, the European benchmark, was up as much as 4.3pc to more than €75 per megawatt hour, its highest level since January 2023.
Prices have risen for three days in a row over concerns the latest strikes in the Middle East will disrupt shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, where a fifth of global oil and gas exports usually pass during peacetime.
The US launched its first attacks in more than a month over the weekend.
Constraints on shipping threaten to push up inflation as it limits supplies of goods and energy. Higher inflation tends to trigger higher interest rates and bond yields – a proxy for government borrowing costs.
Jim Reid, an analyst at Deutsche Bank, said: “As meteorological autumn begun yesterday, a chill swept through markets as rising geopolitical risk, oil prices and bond yields created a risk off start to September.
“The fresh catalyst for the sell-off over the last 24 hours was the jump in energy prices.”
Good morning
Thanks for joining me. Government borrowing costs have continued to rise after the US launched fresh attacks on Iran. Here is what you need to know.
5 things to start your day
1) Bond markets turn on Burnham | Borrowing costs soar to highest in decades, leaving Prime Minister facing £14bn Budget shortfall
2) London Stock Exchange turns to crypto in push to revive market | LSE’s tokenised equities are the latest attempt to attract traders and boost City’s competitiveness
3) Sky accuses ex-Bake Off boss of double-counting costs in accounts row | Broadcaster alleges TV producer inappropriately used corporate credit card for personal expenses
4) M&S and Tesco warn Burnham against high street tax raid | Retailers urge Prime Minister not to increase levies on large shops at time of rising costs
5) Hundreds of workers to sue over Lindsey Oil Refinery’s collapse | Union officials seek possible taxpayer-funded £6,000 payouts for employees of insolvent firm
What happened overnight
Oil prices surged following fresh escalations in the US-Iran war.
The price of Brent crude jumped by more than 5pc on Tuesday to a five-week high above $95 per barrel, and remained above that level overnight.
Asian shares tumbled Wednesday over the turmoil in the Middle East and as the bond market sell-off deepened globally.
The yield on 10-year bonds in Japan, Australia and the US all rose to fresh multi-year highs.
Tokyo’s Nikkei 225 stock market dropped 3pc to 64,278.95. SoftBank Group, the Japanese multinational investment holding firm which invests in OpenAI, fell 6.3pc.
South Korea’s Kospi lost 3.6pc to 6,588.95, with Samsung down 3.3pc and memory chipmaker SK Hynix down 3.5pc.
Hong Kong’s Hang Seng slipped 0.8pc to 25,126.40, and the Shanghai Composite index dipped 0.9pc to 3,943.22.
Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 fell 1.1pc to 8,971.90 and Taiwan’s Taiex dropped 1.5pc.
US stocks slumped on Tuesday as the global bond sell-off deepened and oil prices jumped.
All three American stock indexes fell on Tuesday. The S&P 500 dropped by 0.7pc, the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell by 0.8pc and the tech-heavy Nasdaq Composite was down by 1pc.
Investors are now pricing in a 68pc chance of a Federal Reserve interest rate rise at the central bank’s meeting this month, up from 40pc a week ago.
summary: Bond traders have warned that Prime Minister Andy Burnham risks a Liz Truss-style market meltdown unless he presents a credible spending and funding plan ahead of next month's Budget. UK borrowing costs have surged to multi-decade highs amid a global bond market sell-off, while Mr Burnham has refused to rule out increasing borrowing or taxes. Investors and economists emphasize that the government must demonstrate control over public spending and welfare costs to reassure the markets and lower yields.
key_points: Bond traders warned that Prime Minister Andy Burnham risks a Liz Truss-style market meltdown over a lack of credible spending plans.
UK borrowing costs surged to multi-decade highs amid a global bond market sell-off and escalating conflict in the Middle East.
Mr Burnham refused to rule out increasing borrowing or taxes during his first Prime Minister's Questions.
Investors and economists state that the market wants to see spending cuts and a clear recognition of unsustainable welfare spending.
The number of children living in workless homes climbed to a 12-year high of 1.54 million in the three months to June.

title: Faisal Islam: Why bond market wildfire is keeping world leaders up at night
author: Faisal Islam
content:
![An American flag waves against a backdrop of cranes and storage containers in Los Angeles.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/2560/cpsprodpb/47b0/live/d36b9110-a6cb-11f1-a291-b542ee92de7c.jpg)
- Published
It is not just the wildfire burning in the bond markets, with many countries facing interest rates at multi-decade highs.
The markets lending money to governments appear to be changing more fundamentally too.
Over summer, the message has been made clear: countries will have to pay more to borrow cash.
The immediate reason is the ongoing closure of the Strait of Hormuz and renewed hostilities between the US and Iran, which has pushed up inflation and, in turn, raised expectations of higher interest rates in the world's major economies.
Markets had assumed tensions would subside, and so too would oil and gas prices, ahead of the US midterm elections in November.
It was wishful thinking, based on the hope that US President Donald Trump would want the conflict in the Middle East resolved well before Americans go to the polls.
But that has not happened, leaving markets pricing in higher energy prices, a chronic Gulf crisis, higher inflation for longer - and so higher interest rates.
![A line chart showing yields on government 10-year bonds from 2006 to 2026, with four lines representing the UK, US, France, and Japan. The UK is the focal point as it has higher numbers at the beginning and end of the time series. To start with, the UK figure is around 4.4%, falls a little, then rises steeply to a high of 5.46% in 2007. The figures then gradually undulate down to a low of 0.17% in mid 2020, before rising fairly rapidly again to a recent peak of over 5.2% in September 2026. By comparison, the US follows a very similar trajectory just below the UK from 2006 to the late 2010s, before diverging and staying several percentage points higher than the UK, hovering around 3.0% by 2018. The latest value for the US is around 4.8% in September 2026. France also tracks the UK quite closely, though it falls below the UK in the years leading up to the pandemic. The latest value for September 2026 is around 4.2%. Japan stays notably lower than the other countries in general, staying below 2% from 2006 until very recently, when it hits a new high of 3% in September 2026.](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1600/cpsprodpb/2072/live/810dfc80-a6cd-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.png)
But that is only part of the story.
The bigger picture is rising demand for borrowing across the world - and not just from governments. Big tech companies are turning to the same bond markets to raise hundreds of billions of dollars for investments in AI data centres.
Over $219bn (Â£162bn) of debt has already been issued this year by the US "hyperscalers" such as Google, Amazon and Meta, nearly a third of it in currencies other than the dollar, including sterling.
The total issued last year was $93bn, while before that it averaged less than $40bn a year. Some expect the tech giants to raise $400-$500bn from the bond markets this year. These are staggering sums, raising competition in the market and pushing up the price for governments.
Looking east, there is another major borrower: Japan.
It has the highest debt burden, relative to its GDP, of the major economies and is the biggest single lender to the US government. Until recently its central bank's interest rate was zero, but that has crept up to help combat rising inflation.
As a result, its government bond yields have been pushed to 30-year highs. The declining value of the yen complicates things, but the bottom line is that there is a change afoot in the global flow of money.
The biggest factor pushing up rates is the credibility of the borrowing plans set out by major countries. The increase is not based on fears about countries "going bankrupt".
But it is based on the brutal market equation that if a country wants to borrow more, and to do so without a credible plan, especially if there are doubts over the stability of a given government, it should expect to pay a higher rate.
Influential economists lean on different factors. Mohamed el-Erian told me the AI competition in bond markets was the biggest new factor.
Lord Jim O'Neill, says the recent action has been caused by uncertainty about US policy, and in particular efforts by the US Government to try to manage down surging yields.
This brings us to the UK. The profound and rolling instability of multiple prime ministers, chancellors, policy U-turns and the seeming inability to push through major structural change in this country over the past decades, has attracted a premium.
It was part of Sir Keir Starmer's strategy to try to take on boring reforms and offer markets stability in a bid to lower borrowing costs.
It was a shock to many in the markets that despite a landslide majority, Labour could not push through plans to cut Britain's welfare bill. This added to the ups and downs in the gilt markets - the trade in British government debt.
Actually, there are signs of green shoots in the underlying economy. Economic growth has been faster than peers so far in 2026, despite the energy price spike.
Measures of consumer confidence have ticked back up again. The PM is hoping to build on these signs to help rebuild the economy.
But the ongoing rout in global bond markets raises serious questions about the coherence and detail of Burnham's broader plans.
"More public control" and more support for those struggling with the cost of living sounds like a plan for more spending, while the former could turn off potential investors looking at the country.
Burnham's former economic adviser, Lord O'Neill, told me yesterday that the PM's 10-year plan, expected in November, needs to set out how he will tackle "excessive spending".
Lord O'Neill believes showing investors he can be decisive on the state pension or the welfare bill will give him breathing room to focus on his favoured infrastructure investments.
As interest rates tick up, the trade offs facing the prime minister only get more difficult.
summary: Global bond markets are facing severe pressure as governments and major tech companies compete for massive amounts of borrowing amid geopolitical tensions and rising inflation. The closure of the Strait of Hormuz and US-Iran hostilities have driven up energy prices and long-term interest rate expectations. Meanwhile, massive debt issuance by US tech giants for AI data centres and concerns over government spending plans and political stability are further pushing up borrowing costs worldwide.
key_points: Ongoing conflict between the US and Iran, alongside the closure of the Strait of Hormuz, has driven up inflation and interest rate expectations.
US tech giants have massively increased bond market borrowing to fund AI data centre investments, raising competition and costs for governments.
Japan's bond yields have reached 30-year highs as its central bank raises interest rates to combat inflation.
Markets are demanding higher interest rates from countries that lack credible borrowing plans or stable political leadership.
The UK faces specific market scrutiny and higher borrowing costs due to questions surrounding government spending and structural reforms.

title: Global bond sell-off intensifies as US-Iran tensions stoke inflation fears
author: Heather Stewart
content:
The global government bond sell-off resumed on Wednesday, driving up the UK’s borrowing costs and exacerbating the challenges facing John Healey as he prepares his first budget.
The yield – effectively the interest rate – on 10-year UK government bonds, or gilts, jumped to just below 5.3% in early trading: its highest level since mid-2008.
Investors across major markets have been dumping bonds in recent days amid fears about inflation and spiralling deficits.
Global inflation fears have intensified since the US and Iran began exchanging fire again at the weekend, pushing up the oil price and increasing expectations that central banks will have to raise interest rates in the coming months.
Higher bond yields progressively increase the cost of financing the government’s debt. UK analysts have warned that higher gilt yields since the start of the Iran war have potentially wiped out almost half of Healey’s headroom against the government’s fiscal rules.
Economists at Deutsche Bank reckon the £26bn room for manoeuvre Rachel Reeves created at her spring forecast could be down to less than £14bn by the time of the 28 October budget.
Healey would then have to decide whether to rebuild the margin for error with tax increases or spending cuts – alongside facing pressure to fund higher defence spending.
Chris Beauchamp, the chief market analyst at IG, said: “Governments around the world are feeling the pressure from bond markets, but the situation is particularly acute for the UK, where Andy Burnham’s grand promises about reforming the economy are about to meet the cold reality of high debt levels and rocketing borrowing costs.”
after newsletter promotion
The Brent crude oil benchmark is currently hovering at about $95 a barrel amid renewed fighting in the Middle East. The US launched new airstrikes on Iranian targets overnight, prompting counterstrikes by Tehran targeting American interests in Gulf allies.
The resumption of the sell-off in UK markets came after Asian stock markets fell sharply. In Tokyo the Nikkei 225 share index slumped by 2.85%. China’s CSI 300 lost 1.4%, while South Korea’s Kospi dropped by 3.3%.
