Clay shrinks when it dries out, leading to what Network Rail described as “issues with the quality of the track”.
Martin Beable, chief operating officer of Great British Railways Anglia, which runs c2c and Greater Anglia-branded services, said: “Our teams are working together across Anglia to keep running the best possible service despite the significant challenges we’re facing because of this exceptionally hot and dry weather.
“Thank you for bearing with us, and please do check before you travel, particularly if you’re used to getting the same time train every day.”
summary: Network Rail has imposed speed restrictions and timetable changes on train services in southern Essex starting Tuesday due to the risk of derailments. The restrictions are necessary because ongoing drought conditions have caused clay beneath the railway lines to dry out and shrink, compromising track quality. Following two recent derailments during hot weather, affected services between London and Southend may take up to eight minutes longer than usual.
key_points: Speed restrictions affect c2c and Greater Anglia routes between London and Southend.
The measures are a response to clay beneath the tracks drying and shrinking during the drought.
Two trains derailed in hot weather earlier this month, including one in Essex.
Affected journeys will take up to eight minutes longer than normal.

title: John Caudwell and Stuart Rose blast ‘tax creep’
author: Mauricio Alencar
content:
![John Caudwell in a formal setting, possibly during a business meeting or public speaking event, conveying professionalism.](https://www.cityam.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/06/John-Caudwell.jpg?w=742) 
Billionaire political donor John Caudwell and retail bigwig Lord Stuart Rose have hit out at the “creep of taxes” hitting businesses across the country.
The influential business veterans have joined a campaign led by entrepreneur group Helm calling on the government to “stop the creep of taxes on wealth creators”.
A letter, which has been signed by Pimlico Plumbers’ former boss Charlie Mullins and Gail’s Bakery chairman Luke Johnson, urges Labour to stop rolling out new tax hikes on founders, including levies on dividends, capital gains and business assets.
Lord Rose, the former chairman of Asda and Marks & Spencer, said he had “never been more concerned about the cost of doing business” and added that taxes and regulation had become “serious impediments to growth and employment”.
“Employers’ National Insurance alone took £100m a year out of one supermarket,” Rose said, referring to the impact of former Chancellor Rachel Reeves’ £25bn tax hike in late 2024.
“Multiply that across the economy and it is easy to see why investment has stalled.”
Caudwell separately told the Telegraph he did not believe Labour were “electable” despite being a donor to the party before the last election.
The open letter comes ahead of John Healey’s Budget on 28 October. The new Chancellor has promised to offer businesses “breathing space” after the private sector was hit with a high share of tax hikes under Reeves.
The letter concludes that a “steady creep of tax rises and reductions in entrepreneurial reliefs is making it harder to build and scale a business in the UK”.
Pre-Budget lobbying underway
Economists are raising the alarm on the design of the tax system and the changes that have taken place over the century.
One Westminster think tank argued that the tax system has bcome more damaging for growth in the last 15 years.
The Institute of Economic Affairs (IEA) has said that the overall system has deteriorated over the last 15 years such that incentives for investment have been “eroded”.
Tom Clougherty, former chief of the right-leaning think tank, said twice raising taxes on investment at moments of economic crises was a “major error, and likely had a chilling effect on growth”.
Research suggested that levies on investment – via corporation tax, personal taxes on dividends and capital gains tax changes – have climbed by 10 percentage points since the Great Financial Crisis of 2008.
The new report pins the blame on successive Tory and Labour governments for targeting investors and workers over less productive parts of the economy. Since 2024, the Labour government has cumulatively raised about £65bn in taxes, with more than half impacting businesses.
“The tax system didn’t cause Britain’s growth slowdown, but it has made bouncing back much harder than it needed to be,” Clougherty said.
“Looking back, it seems extraordinary that we have twice responded to major economic crises by sharply raising taxes on investment – but that’s what happened.
“My fear is that on current trends the 2020s and 2030s are going to be much worse in this respect than the 2010s. The tax system is probably a greater threat to enterprise and initiative today than at any point in the last 35 years.”
Taxes hit personal incomes
The paper by the IEA highlights research by the accountancy body ICAEW suggesting that the HMRC handbook has more than tripled in size from 7,250 pages to about 23,500 pages.
Clougherty also argued that the UK would rank above its current level of 32 out of 38 on the Tax Foundation’s International Tax Competitiveness Index had taxes on personal income remained at pre-financial crisis levels.
According to the IEA’s research, the burden on personal income has swollen from 44.5 per cent of government revenue in 2000 to 51 per cent of receipts some 24 years later.
Clougherty pointed out that the number of people paying the additional rate of tax, about 5.5m more since 2000, has been a “striking change” in the UK economy.
The withdrawal of the personal allowance for people earning more than £100,000 hits 500,000 more people than when it was initially introduced.
summary: Billionaire John Caudwell, Lord Stuart Rose, and other prominent business figures have signed an open letter urging the Labour government to halt rising taxes on wealth creators, founders, and investors ahead of the October 28 Budget. The campaign warns that the continuous creep of taxes, regulations, and levies on dividends, capital gains, and business assets severely harms growth, employment, and investment. Meanwhile, a report from the Institute of Economic Affairs cautions that successive governments have eroded investment incentives over the past 15 years, making the UK tax system a major threat to enterprise.
key_points: Business leaders and entrepreneurs signed a letter calling on Labour to stop rolling out new tax hikes on wealth creators, founders, and business assets.
Lord Stuart Rose stated that taxes and regulation have become serious impediments to growth, citing Employers' National Insurance as a major cost.
An Institute of Economic Affairs report warns that levies on investment have climbed by 10 percentage points since the 2008 financial crisis.
The IEA noted that the tax burden on personal income has risen from 44.5 per cent of government revenue in 2000 to 51 per cent.

title: Benefits to cost taxpayer extra £1.7bn, warns IFS
author: Emma Taggart; Szu Ping Chan
content:
![John Healey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499410323_17875613246200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqWS14qhYPBGny4Y46-fINE_4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![John Healey](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000499410323_17875613246200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4BqWS14qhYPBGny4Y46-fINE_4Xpit_DMGvdp2n7FDd82k.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Britain’s benefits bill will rise by an extra £1.7bn if inflation remains high, the Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) has warned, piling pressure on John Healey before the Budget.
The think tank said price rises unleashed by the Iran war will lead to the Chancellor potentially spending £5bn more on benefits, public sector pensions and debt interest.
Prices rose by 2.9pc in the year to July, well above the Bank of England’s 2pc target.
Most economists expect inflation to rise even further this year as the US vows to step up economic pressure on Tehran, prolonging the conflict in the Middle East.
In a move that will increase inflationary pressures on households, Ofgem, the energy regulator, is expected to say on Wednesday that typical gas and electricity bills will rise by 4pc in October to £1,729, up £66 from £1,663 in July.
This threatens to push up inflation further, undermining Andy Burnham’s pledge to bring down the cost of living.
The IFS said that if inflation remained at 2.9pc into the autumn, Mr Healey would still have to find an extra £1.7bn from 2027-28 onwards if he chooses to raise benefits payments in line with price rises.
This is equivalent to funding more than 20 new fighter jets or 25,000 soldiers’ salaries at a time when Mr Healey, the former defence secretary, faces calls to spend more on Britain’s military.
Working-age benefits are usually uprated in line with September’s inflation rate. The Office for Budget Responsibility, the government’s tax and spending watchdog, predicted before the war that inflation would stand at 2.1pc.
Inflation at 2.9pc would also mean spending on public sector pensions would rise by around £0.7bn, the IFS added.
However, the biggest effect will be on the Government’s ballooning debt interest bill, which is tied to the retail prices index. This will rise by as much as £2.3bn if this measure of inflation remains close to current levels.
In total, this could leave the Chancellor facing an additional bill of up to £4.7bn to meet demands, straining the nation’s finances further.
The bill from inflation-linked spending would leave the Government with less funds to provide support for households and businesses affected by rising energy costs.
Pressure from government departments to top up Whitehall spending budgets is also likely to put Mr Healey on a collision course with other Cabinet ministers.
This is because these budgets are set in cash terms, meaning higher inflation erodes their value.
Economists believe inflation is likely to breach 3pc in the coming months, which would force Andrew Bailey, the Governor of the Bank of England, to write a letter to the Chancellor explaining why inflation is so far above target.
Alexander Harvey, of Oxford Economics, believes inflation will climb to 3.5pc by the end of the year, which would add billions more to public spending.
Britain spent £111.2bn on debt interest last year but the IFS estimates that higher inflation could add £1.8bn in extra costs to index-linked debt this year and up to £0.5bn next year.
However, the think tank said that Mr Healey could raise £1bn in additional tax revenue because the rates for some taxes, including business rates and alcohol duties, are tied to inflation.
The interest on student loan repayments is also tied to the retail price index, which climbed to 3.2pc in July.
Warnings that higher inflation will increase government spending by £4.7bn come as economists estimate that Mr Healey’s fiscal headroom – a self-imposed guardrail to guide public spending – has shrunk.
Rachel Reeves, the former chancellor, had £23.6bn of headroom against her fiscal targets in the spring. But this is estimated to have fallen as low as £8bn because of inflation and rising borrowing costs, according to the Resolution Foundation.
It adds to the challenge facing Mr Burnham and Mr Healey, whose new Government has pledged to tackle the cost of living while grappling with constrained public finances.
Welfare spending is already on track to hit £353bn, up from £314bn when Labour entered Downing Street in 2024.
A Treasury spokesman said: “Fiscal discipline is the bedrock of economic stability and national security.
“The Chancellor and Prime Minister are in lockstep that the Government will meet the fiscal rules, with a buffer against uncertainty – and that includes getting debt down.
“We’re cutting the deficit faster than any other G7 economy to the lowest level in six years.”
summary: The Institute for Fiscal Studies has warned that persistent high inflation, driven partly by conflict in the Middle East, could add an extra £1.7bn to Britain's benefits bill and up to £4.7bn in total to government spending. Price rises are also expected to increase costs for public sector pensions and debt interest, putting severe pressure on the Chancellor ahead of the Budget. Economists predict inflation will climb further in the coming months, eroding the value of department budgets and shrinking fiscal headroom.
key_points: Britain's benefits bill could rise by an extra £1.7bn if inflation remains at 2.9pc into the autumn.
Higher inflation could increase total government spending by up to £4.7bn, including public sector pensions and debt interest.
Ofgem is expected to announce that typical gas and electricity bills will rise by 4pc in October to £1,729.
Inflation is projected by economists to breach 3pc and potentially climb to 3.5pc by the end of the year.
The Chancellor's fiscal headroom has reportedly shrunk from £23.6bn down to as low as £8bn due to inflation and rising borrowing costs.

title: Richard Branson’s plan to make the Eurostar feel like a second-class service
author: Christopher Jasper
content:
![Computer generated picture of a Virgin train at St Pancras International station](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000498685114_17875728024660_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqc_R-fZbnPPOo5bCoTTw0OuLUFsZY-6ahzSUzVgifUsg.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Computer generated picture of a Virgin train at St Pancras International station](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/business/2026/08/24/TELEMMGLPICT000498685114_17875728024660_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqc_R-fZbnPPOo5bCoTTw0OuLUFsZY-6ahzSUzVgifUsg.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Sir Richard Branson’s much touted plan to bring some of the glamour of Virgin Atlantic to his own version of the Eurostar has been derided as a pipe dream by critics.
Overcrowding at St Pancras, a chronic lack of suitable train-maintenance sites and the inevitable mountain of red tape have been viewed as almost insurmountable obstacles to anyone intent on ending Eurostar’s monopoly over services through the Channel tunnel.
But after securing permission to run 20 trains a day between London and the Continent from Britain’s rail regulator, the billionaire’s Virgin Trains is finally beginning to win over doubters.
Virgin must still negotiate access to the tunnel itself, as well as tracks in France, Belgium and the Netherlands. And it faces a nervous wait for a fleet of 12 as yet untested high-speed trains on order from manufacturer Alstom.
However, a ruling from regulators at the Office of Rail and Road (ORR) last week suggests Sir Richard may be about to make good on his ambition of returning to Britain’s railways after Virgin Trains lost the West Coast Main Line franchise in 2019.
![Sir Richard Branson at St Pancras International station](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000446904194_17874815595350_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqaxc0yOCWITeJw1uajCk_kGWo-KAdI1N_TSsvo9Yxjxc.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
Virgin Trains is not the only operator intent on challenging Eurostar’s 31-year monopoly.
Italy’s state-owned Trenitalia announced earlier this month a €2bn (£1.7bn) order for 19 new trains, around half of which it aims to deploy on Channel tunnel services, while a clutch of other would-be operators are also drawing up proposals.
If those plans come to fruition, competition on the route could explode within five years, which could have an impact matching that of the 1990s discount-airline boom.
Plunging fares may encourage an influx of new customers and further loosen the grip of airlines on routes such as London to Paris, where Eurostar already has 80pc of the market.
Train services from London are likely to reach further into Europe, with lower ticket prices making rail competitive as far as Germany, Switzerland and even Italy for travellers with time on their hands.
Mark Smith, a former ORR and Department for Transport executive who runs the Man in Seat 61 travel website, reckons ticket prices could drop by close to a third.
“You’d be looking at more capacity, higher service standards and fares that could be 30pc lower based on what we have seen with the advent of competition in Italy and Spain,” he says.
“That will in turn drive further market share gains for rail compared with the airlines and make it feasible to travel further into Europe on a single ticket.”
Customer service front and centre
Virgin has so far been tight-lipped on what the Channel tunnel service might look like, with Phil Whittingham, its project lead, saying only that the route is “ripe for change” and that Sir Richard intended to build a “premium customer experience on board”.
A spokesman adds: “We don’t want to ruin the element of surprise, but just as we’ve done with Virgin Atlantic and our holidays and hotels offering, you can expect bold ideas with the customer experience front and centre.”
On Virgin Atlantic, that experience has included in-flight bar and massages, with a shift to focusing on tech innovation in recent years, including free Wi-Fi from Elon Musk’s Starlink and an AI-powered virtual concierge.
Virgin has specified single-decker trains for its purchase from Alstom, with one insider suggesting that they were more compatible with providing a full at-seat meal service than the double-deckers with which Eurostar is renewing its fleet.
Virgin has said it intends to operate an initial six return trains a day between London and Paris starting in October 2030, later increasing to 13, followed by four to Brussels and three to Amsterdam.
That would represent a substantial increase on the current timetable, with Eurostar offering 14 daily services to Paris, eight or nine to Brussels and five to Amsterdam.
The company, owned by French state railway SNCF, said Virgin’s plan confirmed “the huge potential for growth in international rail” and that it intended to “play a full part in that growth”.
Jon Worth, an expert in European railways, says Virgin had impressed with its work to secure access to St Pancras, the line to the tunnel and the last remaining space at Temple Mills maintenance shed near Stratford before Trenitalia.
“Seeing this project through has been like threading the eye of a needle,” he adds. “Forget the rhetoric from Branson about transforming travel. They’ve been very methodical and very clear headed in devising a project that will just about fit with all these restrictions.”
![An aerial photograph shows the Temple Mills International train depot](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000487194674_17874818774400_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bqadu-bubCwwNTr_YiFtRU6zzhxYwwKH5sUws766CzosU.jpeg?imwidth=350) 
No room for slippage
However, he says Virgin had taken a risk in choosing a bespoke version of a train built by Alstom in Italy which has not yet been approved in France, introducing the “nightmare” scenario of the trains not being ready for 2030.
Any slippage could open the door to Trenitalia, which is viewed as among the most aggressive of European high-speed operators.
Trenitalia’s train order, from Hitachi Rail, adds to an existing commitment with the Japanese manufacturer and will provide guaranteed delivery times, potentially beating Virgin to the market by a year.
Worth says Trenitalia is likely to expand on routes such as Paris to Lyon and Marseilles and Milan, rather than focusing on London.
Eurostar’s switch to double-deckers for an order of up to 50 new trains may also be problematic, he adds, since the Celestia model is not currently compliant with evacuation requirements within the tunnel in the event of fire.
It is likely that a significant number of the new trains will instead be used on the Paris-Brussels route that Eurostar took over in 2022, easing the pressure on Virgin.
Waiting in the wings are Evolyn, backed by Spanish industrialist Jorge Cosmen, an investor in the owner of National Express, the Dutch startup Heuro, and UK-based Gemini, which has proposed running trains from Stratford and Ebbsfleet to avoid the St Pancras bottleneck.
According to Smith, of the Man in Seat 61 website, Virgin’s best bet will be to play to its strengths by offering upmarket food and wine, exploring initiatives such as allowing carriage of bicycles and dogs, which is currently banned from most Eurostar services.
He says: “It’s that hard-to-define Virgin pizazz that people most want to see and they’ll need to bring that to these trains.”
summary: Sir Richard Branson's Virgin Trains has secured permission from Britain's rail regulator to run 20 daily trains between London and the Continent, aiming to challenge Eurostar's 31-year monopoly. The ambitious venture plans to introduce a customer-focused service starting with London-to-Paris routes by October 2030, potentially lowering ticket prices and expanding international rail options. However, Virgin still faces hurdles, including negotiating access to the Channel tunnel and foreign tracks, as well as awaiting delivery of untested Alstom trains.
key_points: Virgin Trains secured regulatory approval from the ORR to operate 20 trains a day between London and the Continent.
The new service plans to launch in October 2030 with routes to Paris, followed by Brussels and Amsterdam.
Competition from Virgin and other operators like Trenitalia could potentially lower ticket prices by nearly a third.
Virgin has ordered 12 untested high-speed single-decker trains from Alstom to support its premium service offering.

title: Nvidia’s mounting debt pile alarms traders
author: Chris Price
content:
That is despite Wall Street estimates that Nvidia’s revenues will nearly double when it reports its next set of quarterly results on Wednesday. Analysts believe the $5.2tn (£3.8tn) company’s sales will top $92bn.
Nvidia’s swap prices have soared on the back of a series of complex financing deals intended to pay for trillions of dollars in AI data centres.
The company’s debt levels jumped this summer after it raised $25bn in its largest-ever bond-market fundraising in June.
Jensen Huang, Nvidia’s chief executive, announced $500bn of AI financing deals this month with six Wall Street giants, which would see the lenders create special funding vehicles to back large data centres.
Nvidia confirmed last week that it had agreed to backstop a large US data centre being built by OpenAI with up to $105bn in credit support. It has also announced a $500bn deal with South Korean memory chip giant SK Hynix.
Michael Burry, the US investor depicted in the film The Big Short, has claimed that some of Nvidia’s debt deals are “unnatural” and a kind of “circular” financing.
Costs for insuring debt have soared across the technology industry. Swap prices for other infrastructure giants, including Oracle and Broadcom, have also risen to record levels.
Patrick Perret-Green, the chief executive of advisory firm PPG Macro, said the CDS prices were “quite remarkable” given the apparent strength of the industry.
Benedict Keim, a portfolio manager at Altana Wealth, said investors were increasingly watching the “strong correlation” between Nvidia and the wider AI sector, which is heavily loss-making and has been fuelled by borrowing.
He added that the “vast scale” of the credit guarantees that Nvidia was offering to other AI labs had “increased concerns over its future cash flow and credit risk”.
There are also concerns over Nvidia’s role in allegedly circular financing deals. These risked creating “cascading losses through the ecosystem and increasing the probability of systemic risks in the future”, Mr Keim said.
Amish Patel, the head of equity research at Raymond James, added: “The rise in Nvidia’s CDS reflects growing scrutiny of the company’s expanding role in financing the AI ecosystem.”
Nvidia is considering investing in AI start-up Perplexity, which The Information values at $30bn.
Nvidia was contacted for comment.
summary: Nvidia's mounting debt and complex financing deals for AI data centres have raised concerns among traders and analysts despite expectations of surging revenues. The company recently raised $25bn in bond-market fundraising and announced massive AI financing agreements, including credit support for OpenAI. This heavy borrowing and use of credit guarantees have driven up debt-insuring swap prices and sparked fears of potential systemic risks and future credit strain.
key_points: Nvidia raised $25bn in its largest-ever bond-market fundraising in June.
CEO Jensen Huang announced $500bn in AI financing deals with Wall Street lenders.
Nvidia agreed to provide up to $105bn in credit support for an OpenAI data centre.
Investors and analysts have raised concerns over circular financing and potential systemic risks.

title: Thames Water creditors accused of ‘shuffling chairs on Titanic’ with plan for new board
author: Alex Daniel
content:
The group of creditors pursuing a rescue bid for Thames Water have been accused of shuffling the deckchairs on the Titanic after proposing an overhaul of the stricken utility’s board.
In a bid to stave off temporary nationalisation by Andy Burnham, the lenders said they would appoint Liz Barber, the former chief executive of Yorkshire Water, and Clive Selley, the former chief executive of network operator Openreach, as directors if they are allowed to take formal control of the company.
London & Valley Water (L&VW), a consortium of 100 institutional investors holding £17bn of the company’s £21bn debt, has also lined up Dame Bernadette Kelly, the former permanent secretary of the Department for Transport.
Mike McTighe, the corporate troubleshooter leading Thames’s overhaul, would become the new chair, replacing the incumbent Sir Adrian Montague, if Thames is able to get its £10bn rescue deal approved by the government. McTighe is the current chair of Openreach.
He said: “The challenge at Thames Water is huge. If this recapitalisation plan is accepted, we will apply full dedication as a new board, working alongside the executive team to transform the business and build a culture in which the customers and local communities who depend on Thames Water come first.”
The proposed appointments are designed to reassure the government that any commercial deal would bring with it a leadership overhaul, as Burnham’s team examines the possibility of taking the company back into public ownership.
L&VW’s announcement was criticised by the public ownership campaign group We Own It. Cat Hobbs, the director at We Own It, said: “This is absolutely absurd. A cosy stitch-up that has nothing to do with the interests of the 16 million people who depend on Thames Water. This amounts to nothing more than a reshuffling of chairs on the deck of the Titanic.”
Burnham has said there should be “greater public control” of Thames Water and previously told the Guardian this could mean nationalisation. This would probably come via placing the company into a special administration regime (SAR), a form of temporary nationalisation.
More recently the prime minister said he was “angry” after companies including Thames Water were given the green light to raise bills even higher earlier this month.
He said the companies must not be allowed to treat bill payers like a “blank cheque”, an escalation of his warnings to utility companies that he is looking at options for more government control of the sector.
The SAR proposal would transfer the costs of running the company to the taxpayer, with Thames Water claiming the bill could come to £2bn.
L&VW, which includes fund managers such as Apollo Global Management, Elliott Management, Farallon Capital Management and Silver Point Capital, has also moved to strengthen its legal position in order to be prepared if Thames is nationalised.
after newsletter promotion
The consortium has hired the top litigation and disputes lawyers Pallas Partners to work alongside Akin Gump, the law firm advising the consortium on the terms of their restructuring proposals.
The lenders have been trying to take ownership and bring Thames out of administration after a failed attempt to sell the utility to the US investment group KKR last year.
However, the creditors’ plans were thrown into doubt in June when Emma Reynolds, the then environment secretary, wrote to the regulator, Ofwat, voicing concerns about the terms of the deal.
McTighe said the 10-year plan to turn the water company around would “fix the foundations” at Thames. “It will take time to fix Thames Water, but we are committed to rebuilding trust with the customers and public Thames Water serves,” he said.
Russ Mould, the investment director at AJ Bell, said of the proposed new appointments: “The hope being that these are the sort of credible names which can inspire confidence in the company’s future in private hands.
“Such an outcome would impose large losses on creditors, who are seeking to formally take ownership of the business, having already assumed de facto control, with plans to list it on the stock market as early as 2030.”
summary: Creditors attempting a rescue bid for Thames Water have proposed a leadership overhaul to prevent temporary nationalisation. The consortium, London & Valley Water, has named figures including former Yorkshire Water chief executive Liz Barber and Mike McTighe for new board roles. However, public ownership campaigners criticised the plan as a superficial move, while the government continues to weigh options for increased public control.
key_points: A consortium of creditors holding £17bn of Thames Water's debt has proposed a new board, including Mike McTighe as chair and former Yorkshire Water CEO Liz Barber as a director.
The proposed leadership overhaul aims to reassure the government and stave off temporary nationalisation via a special administration regime.
Campaign group We Own It criticised the plan as an absurd "cosy stitch-up" and likened it to shuffling chairs on the Titanic.
The prime minister has warned that utility companies must not treat bill payers like a blank cheque amid ongoing scrutiny of the sector.

title: Graduate job vacancies drop by almost 50% in a year, survey suggests
author: Emer Moreau
content:
![A young woman in a modern office at a table with a co-worker](https://ichef.bbci.co.uk/ace/standard/1920/cpsprodpb/7356/live/324f6630-9fb4-11f1-aed2-8d6da8d75094.jpg)
Adzuna said the number of graduate vacancies was the lowest since it started recording in 2016
- Published
The number of graduate jobs has fallen almost in half in the past year, according to new figures, as employers cut entry-level roles in favour of AI and battle rising costs.
Jobs website Adzuna said it had just 8,383 graduate vacancies listed in July, down from 15,397 at the same point last year.
Adzuna also found competition among job seekers across all levels is rising, with an average of 2.14 job seekers per vacancy in July, up from 1.93 a year earlier.
Businesses have said employer national insurance and minimum wage hikes have made hiring more expensive, particularly for junior staff.
The number of graduate vacancies listed hit its lowest level since Adzuna started recording such data in 2016. The firm pointed to a peak for graduate roles in 2017, when it had more than 55,800 listed on its website. That is more than six times the number of roles listed on the site in July.
Andrew Hunter, the co-founder of Adzuna, said the figures show "employers still haven't found a reason to open up hiring" for recent graduates.
Official figures show the UK's youth unemployment rate - which covers 16-to-24-year-olds - was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026. The number of young people not in education, employment or training (Neet) is now over one million.
Young people have told BBC News previously they have applied for hundreds of jobs before even receiving a response.
They also expressed frustration at the growing number of employers using AI to screen applications.
Many university graduates also face mounting student debt.
Former government minister Alan Milburn is leading a major review of the youth unemployment crisis. He has previously said the number of entry-level jobs is shrinking, as is the number of part-time jobs traditionally filled by teenagers and students.
The Adzuna data also showed vacancies for jobs in travel, teaching and construction rose in recent weeks.
But sectors including healthcare, nursing, hospitality and logistics posted fewer vacancies.
Prime Minister Andy Burnham recently changed the rules for public contracts so that companies bidding for them have to show how they will create jobs and training opportunities.
summary: According to data from the jobs website Adzuna, graduate job vacancies have fallen by nearly 50% over the past year to the lowest level since records began in 2016. Employers are cutting entry-level roles and turning to artificial intelligence amid rising costs driven by national insurance and minimum wage hikes. Meanwhile, overall competition for jobs is rising, and the UK's youth unemployment rate reached 16.2% in the three months leading to March 2026.
key_points: Graduate vacancies dropped to 8,383 in July, down from 15,397 the previous year.
Rising hiring costs, including minimum wage and national insurance hikes, have contributed to employers cutting junior roles.
Competition among job seekers increased to an average of 2.14 applicants per vacancy in July.
Official figures indicate the UK youth unemployment rate was 16.2% in the three months to March 2026.
While graduate, healthcare, and hospitality vacancies fell, roles in travel, teaching, and construction saw increases.

title: The AI reckoning is coming, it’s just a matter of timing
author: Andrew Orlowski
content:
![Michael Burry at the "The Big Short" New York premiere](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000345979051_17874868656200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq0quQUhCPHdUHY_XWT5Ck7ziIXdNr9atEw2H4ySp7WWI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
![Michael Burry at the "The Big Short" New York premiere](https://www.telegraph.co.uk/content/dam/briefs/2026/08/23/TELEMMGLPICT000345979051_17874868656200_trans_NvBQzQNjv4Bq0quQUhCPHdUHY_XWT5Ck7ziIXdNr9atEw2H4ySp7WWI.jpeg?imwidth=640) 
Timing is everything, and fortunes can be made or lost predicting when a bubble will burst.
In 2005, the contrarian hedge fund boss Michael Burry bet against the US mortgage market. Incontinent lenders had approved mortgages to people with little or no income, and had even extended the credit, rolling up the interest into the principal balance. The lenders then sold on these mortgages, which were obscured by securitisation.
But Burry had to wait. As one account put it, he “needed to lay his chips on the table now and wait for the casino to wake up and change the odds of the game”.
It was obvious in hindsight that a small change in the cost of these loans, or the loanees’ ability to pay them, would change things. But it didn’t very much, and as months turned into years, Burry almost lost the lot. However, a reckoning can only be delayed so long. Ultimately a rotten superstructure is maintained only by confidence, and when this evaporates the edifice collapses overnight.
Burry has bet against the AI bubble, and once again he must wait. A staggering proportion of the stock market’s rise since 2022 comes from AI-related companies. While this year’s decline has caught out reckless, quasi-religious believers in AI such as the 24-year old Leopold Aschenbrenner, whose hedge fund collapsed from $45bn to $10bn (£33bn to £7bn) because he bet on the market only going up, it hasn’t become a full-blown rout.
The conventional wisdom is that one company at the centre of the bubble remains relatively impregnable: Nvidia. For the past two years Nvidia has swapped places with Apple as the world’s most valuable company, valued at around $5tn. Nvidia makes the most advanced microprocessors in the world, allowing AI to do more things faster, and it can charge a premium for this valuable product.
Nvidia benefits from the “picks and shovels” idiom. Which is to say that in a gold rush, the smartest investment is in the people who sell mining equipment to the gold prospectors. It doesn’t matter if nobody finds gold. The names on the AI model leadership boards may rise and fall, and favourites may come in and fall out of fashion, but everyone in AI needs Nvidia’s chips to produce the best benchmark results.
Its strength looks even more impregnable considering the difficulties AI model companies like Anthropic or OpenAI are experiencing in building a “competitive moat”. Features are rapidly copied by cheap, open rivals which businesses can run at a much lower cost. Billions spent on R&D almost instantly vanish.
Burry isn’t buying it. He’s short on Nvidia, and last week identified a new Achilles heel. A startup chip rival called Etched he says can produce “10x the performance at lower cost per die” – the manufacturing cost to produce a single functional microchip.
Venture capital is pouring into semiconductor companies that address what is called the “inference bottleneck”, the calculations performed after you’ve sent your prompt. This column has highlighted a few, including British companies Fractile and Olix.
Another was touted by the bullish AI pundit Andrew Côté last week. This is particularly intriguing, as it relates to a classic ploy used by computer companies from IBM to Microsoft to create an impregnable defence: compatibility.
To deter competition, back in the mainframe era, IBM was able to design the socket interfaces by which rivals could attach their own equipment. Those that succeeded, like the company Amdahl, were deemed “plug compatible”.
In the software era, Microsoft defined and controlled the application programming interfaces (APIs), which are really plugs and sockets into the software platform beneath, on which applications are built. Microsoft could easily move the goalposts too, and application developers who were wary of the risk of things breaking chose to stick with Microsoft, even when cheaper alternatives arose.
Nvidia’s great strength today derives from such a socket interface or API called CUDA. For developers who build AI models and applications, CUDA is the only game in town, and for two decades tools have been built on top of that interface.
It’s notable that China, which is desperate for the latest Nvidia chips despite a US embargo, nevertheless forbids its developers from using CUDA. It doesn’t want them getting hooked.
AI infrastructure agent Infinity is using teams of AI agents to optimise models on specific hardware, a job that was simply not worth attempting using expert human labour, but that can yield performance results. CUDA may be made redundant.
Nvidia’s financial strength has been used to finance the data centre build out, which Burry doesn’t like one bit.
According to The Economist, the data centre splurge requires $2.5tn in annual AI revenue to break even. The more sceptical former IMF and Goldman Sachs analyst Peter Berezin believes even $10tn may be low.
Both agree demand can’t match the investment. The big experiments on agentic AI have not worked out, as it is too unreliable. While AI waits for the lucrative mass-market applications investors need, those data centres are depreciating rapidly, and innovations identified by Burry and Côté could render them expensive stranded assets.
Of course, Burry has been wrong before, but was he definitively wrong, or just too early? As John Maynard Keynes warned, the market can stay irrational longer than you can stay solvent.
summary: Hedge fund manager Michael Burry has placed a short bet against the current artificial intelligence boom, drawing parallels to his famous 2005 bet against the US mortgage market. While companies like Nvidia have dominated the market by supplying essential microprocessors and dominating software interfaces like CUDA, critics argue that massive data centre investments will struggle to break even. Emerging chip rivals, changing industry standards, and the high costs of infrastructure could threaten Nvidia's stronghold and trigger an AI market correction.
key_points: Michael Burry has bet against the AI bubble, echoing his contrarian short against the US mortgage market in 2005.
Nvidia's high valuation is supported by its advanced microprocessors and its dominant software interface, CUDA.
Data centre build-outs require trillions in annual AI revenue to break even, raising concerns about overinvestment and stranded assets.
Emerging startup chip rivals and alternative optimization technologies threaten to undermine Nvidia's market dominance and render current infrastructure obsolete.
